summary: Kern County is larger than New Jersey — over 8,100 square miles stretching from the southern tip of the San Joaquin Valley up into the Tehachapi Mountains and the fringes of the Mojave Desert — yet it holds fewer than a million people, yielding a density of just 113 per square mile. That sprawl means radically different landscapes within one county line: flat, irrigated farmland around Bakersfield, wind-turbine-studded passes near Tehachapi, and stark high-desert terrain to the east. The economy runs on oil extraction, agriculture, logistics, and a significant military presence at Edwards Air Force Base, giving the county a surprisingly varied employment base where switching industries doesn't necessarily mean switching counties. Housing is the headline draw: a median home value of $310,600 against a median household income of $67,660 produces a price-to-income ratio around 4.6 — remarkable for California, where coastal counties routinely hit 8 or higher — and median rent sits at $1,220 a month. The tradeoff is real, though: a 19% poverty rate signals that affordability coexists with economic strain, and the violent crime rate of 607 per 100,000 sits well above national averages. With an annual average of 10 hours of daily sunshine and daytime highs averaging 75°F, summer heat in the valley is relentless, routinely topping 100°F for weeks. Kern is essentially California's interior bargain — genuinely cheap by state standards, genuinely hot, and defined less by a single city center than by the vast, oil-and-agriculture landscape connecting its scattered communities.
